At the same time, part of the boil-off gas may be fed to the ship’s engines provided they operate on LNG (dual-fuel engines) through cryogenic pumps and vaporization units, allowing the use of ethane as a clean-burning marine fuel; similarly, ethane could be leveraged in other vehicles provided the boil-off gas fuel is the primary power source or optimized for use in the prime mover. 4.2 Cryogenic Fuel Deployment This section provides a comparison of the three cryogenic fuels (LH , LNG, and LE) and what is 2 similar and different for delivery methods, storage, on-site energy demands for liquefaction, airport-specific considerations, and dispensing to aircraft. Details specific to LH , LNG, and LE 2 follow. As can be noted from Section 4.1, in terms of fuel movement, hydrogen, natural gas, and ethane fuels typically rely on similar transportation methods. Each of these fuels can be delivered via liquid trucks when delivery volumes are low and via pipelines at higher throughput. Although, at typical pipeline pressures, ethane is in a liquid state, while natural gas and hydrogen are gaseous. For international transoceanic delivery, liquefaction followed by ocean carrier shipping is the realistic method of transport. The primary differences among these fuels with respect to transport arise from their different thermal, chemical, and physical properties, which dictate distinct infrastructure requirements and operational procedures. For example, because the hydrogen molecule is much smaller than a methane or ethane molecule (Table 8), more specialized materials must be chosen to transport hydrogen such that it does not permeate through the material and cause embrittlement. This is the case for both pipeline materials and cryogenic storage tanks on board trucks and ocean carriers. When getting into the specifics of cryogenic fuel transport via truck or ocean carrier, we also find that the temperature at which the fuel is stored impacts infrastructure material selection and design. LH is stored at much lower temperatures than LNG or LE which means that insulation 2 performance must be superior for LH storage and transport tanks to limit heat ingress. Another 2 fuel property that causes variation in system design during transport is gas mass density. Specifically, LE truck or ocean carrier operators must be aware that ethane gas is heavier than air, unlike hydrogen and natural gas which are lighter than air at ambient conditions; so, if LE boil-off gas is vented, the system would have to be designed differently than an LNG or LH 2 boil-off gas venting system. In addition, in the case of a leakage event, risk mitigation procedures would be different for a fuel that stays close the ground versus one that rises and disperses. Because of the low density of hydrogen gas, it would disperse the quickest during a leakage event. Finally, differences in volumetric energy density are important to note because fuels with lower volumetric energy density, such as LH , require more shipments (via truck or ship) to 2 deliver the same amount of energy, impacting supply chain logistics and airport operations.
